title: Changing Identities and Evolving Conceptions of Inquiry through Teacher-Driven Professional Development
extended_summary:
This paper examines how a small group of secondary science teachers changed their conceptions of classroom scientific inquiry and their participation in a teacher-researcher professional community. The core question is whether a teacher-driven professional development model can help teachers develop a more coherent, expert-like understanding of inquiry while also increasing their agency and leadership within the community.

The intervention was Streamline to Mastery, a five-year professional development program in which teachers and university researchers met every other week, shared lessons, reflected on inquiry-oriented instruction, discussed classroom experiences, and collaboratively shaped the agenda. The teachers were from two urban high schools in the Rocky Mountain West and taught physics or physical science; three of the four taught outside their scientific discipline. Data included lesson reflections, survey responses, meeting videos, email threads, and interviews.

The study concludes that the teachers' talk about inquiry became increasingly aligned with the NRC inquiry framework over time, and that they jointly developed a shared definition of inquiry. The paper also reports growing teacher participation, including more teacher-initiated email threads, more teacher-led agenda setting, and more challenging of one another's ideas. The authors argue that sustained, teacher-centered discourse grounded in classroom experience supported both conceptual growth and the emergence of a community of practice, though the study notes that coherent implementation of inquiry in classroom practice was not empirically verified.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative single-group study of four teachers, not a causal comparison study of an AI intervention in K-12 science. It provides descriptive evidence about professional learning and discourse change, but it does not meet experimental or quasi-experimental credibility criteria.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests a positive developmental trajectory in teacher inquiry discourse and agency, but the evidence is very small-scale, non-causal, and not about student outcomes or AI tools. Any broader thesis about AI-powered tools in K-12 science cannot be supported from this paper; at most, it supports a narrow claim that sustained, collaborative, teacher-driven reflection may improve teachers’ shared understanding of inquiry in a small professional community.

finding.finding_summary: This is not a K-12 student AI-tool causal comparison study; it is a teacher professional development case study about conceptions of scientific inquiry. The teachers’ inquiry talk became more aligned with the NRC inquiry framework over time: references to explanatory and communicative features increased across lesson reflections and survey administrations, but no delayed post-test, transfer task, subgroup analysis, or implementation fidelity measures were reported.
finding.measure: Teacher written reflections, inquiry survey responses, meeting video discourse coding

finding.finding_summary: The study reports growth in teacher agency and collaborative discourse, including more teacher-initiated email threads, agenda setting, and challenging of peers’ ideas over the course of the program. These are qualitative/observational findings rather than causal estimates, and no effect size, delayed post-test, or subgroup effects are reported.
finding.measure: Email participation, agenda-setting codes, challenging discourse codes, focus group interview
